note: Establish a five-column blend-oriented train, including the difficult C6 paraffin/naphthene cut, to measure product recovery and cost.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a high-value partial separation train: C4/C5 root, C3/C4 split, C5/C6 split, C6/C7 split, and difficult paraffin/naphthene split; then add heavy-product columns and tune stages/reflux based on measured margins. Step 1: establish five-column base and inspect costs/purities.
C4, C5 and C6 blends avoid costly component-by-component splits. The root and first three cuts should be relatively easy; BBT (n-hexane/methylcyclopentane) needs more stages and reflux. Light C3 mix and all heavier cuts remain unsold initially.

note: Correct the train to five high-value blend cuts, with sharper separation and higher operating pressure to reduce refrigeration cost.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a five-column blend train: root C5/C6, lights C4/C5 then C3/C4, heavies C6-paraffin/(naphthene+C7+), then naphthene/C7+. Step 2: correct all cut points and use moderate reflux/stages at 0.2 pressure drop.
Initial train mis-cut every column and cost $460M/yr for only $274M revenue. C5, C6-paraffin and C6-naphthene blends are worth roughly $614M, $1104M and $397M/yr at full recovery; C3+C4 add ~$237M. Avoid pure-component splits initially. Higher pressure should reduce refrigeration cost.

note: Sharpen all five intended blend cuts and operate at feed pressure to eliminate refrigeration penalties.
notebook:
PLAN: Build five blend products: root C5/C6; lights C4/C5 then C3/C4; heavies C6-paraffin/(naphthene+C7+), then naphthene/C7+. Step 3: enforce the intended cuts with more stages and full feed pressure.
Prior settings left every outlet far below 95%. Correctly recovered blends are worth about C5 $614M, C6-paraffin $1147M, C6-naphthene $396M, C4 $175M and C3 $60M/yr. Root+B alone should be strongly profitable if cuts are clean. Full pressure should avoid cold condensers; assess purity and cost before refining.

note: Restore convergence with milder root and heavy-column conditions and reduce the plant to the most valuable C6-paraffin cut.
notebook:
PLAN: First restore a convergent, profitable root C5-/C6+ split and C6-paraffin recovery; then add blend cuts one at a time and optimize costs. Step 4: reduce severity, use modest pressure drop, and temporarily sell unqualified leaves.
Five-column sharp designs at zero pressure drop failed at the root. Prior low-pressure designs converged but were impure and costly. Focus now on the high-value C6-paraffin blend (~$1147M/yr potential), with only two columns, to establish a valid baseline before rebuilding C5, C4/C3 and naphthene recovery.

note: Sharpen the C5-/C6+ split and the C6-paraffin cut substantially, aiming to qualify both high-value blend products.
notebook:
PLAN: Establish a profitable C5-/C6+ split and C6-paraffin blend recovery, then add only blend cuts whose revenue exceeds their cost and optimize severity. Step 5: sharpen both existing columns while retaining 0.1 pressure drop for convergence.
The prior root sent about half the C5 material into B, poisoning both intended products; B itself also had excessive refluxing across the C6 paraffin/naphthene boundary. C6 paraffin blend has about $1147M/yr feed value, so this two-column train is the highest-value starting point.

note: Drive both key cuts hard enough to produce sellable C5-minus tops and a C6-paraffin blend, establishing the purity-versus-cost frontier.
notebook:
PLAN: Establish a profitable C5-/C6+ split and C6-paraffin blend recovery, then add only blend cuts whose revenue exceeds their cost and optimize severity. Step 6: force both blend products above 95% with much stronger internal flows, then back off to control cost.
At 70/4 and 60/3 the root leaked roughly 390 mol/s C5 into B and neither product qualified. The C6-paraffin blend is worth about $1147M/yr in the feed, enough to justify a sharp two-column train if total annual cost can be held well below that. No sale yet means recovery/specification, not incremental tuning, is the immediate priority.

note: Use very high root boil-up to strip residual pentane from the C6+ feed, and sharpen the C6-paraffin overhead cut at feed pressure.
notebook:
PLAN: Establish a profitable C5-/C6+ split and C6-paraffin blend recovery, then add only blend cuts whose revenue exceeds their cost and optimize severity. Step 7: force C5 out of the heavy feed and C6 paraffins overhead, then reduce cost after obtaining the first sale.
At 100/10/10 the root still leaked about 88 mol/s light material into B; the C6 column overhead was 83% C6 paraffin, mainly diluted by pentane. Raising root boil-up should attack that dominant impurity more directly than reflux. The C6 blend is worth about $1147M/yr in the feed, so a sharp two-column train can be profitable if costs are subsequently brought well below that. dp=0 avoids refrigeration and previous runs showed it helps cost.

note: Sharpen both cuts and lower pressure to improve relative volatility, targeting a qualifying C6-paraffin overhead before optimizing cost.
notebook:
PLAN: Establish a profitable C5-/C6+ split and C6-paraffin blend recovery, then optimize severity and pressure. Step 8: obtain the first qualifying C6-paraffin blend by sharpening both cuts at moderately reduced pressure, then cut energy once purity is known.
Current 100/10/30 root leaves substantial C6 paraffin in B but B overhead is only about half C6 paraffin: its main contaminants are cyclohexane/MCP and heptane, not merely pentane. Thus B must push naphthenes bottoms as well as exclude heptane. Lower pressure should improve relative volatility enough to offset some refrigeration cost. Maximum root boil-up is retained to strip C5; reflux and stages are increased to keep heavy C6 paraffin from escaping overhead.

note: Switch to the much easier, valuable C5 blend: separate C4-minus overhead, then recover the C5 blend overhead from the bottoms.
notebook:
PLAN: Abandon the difficult C6-paraffin cut; establish a two-column C5-blend train (C4-/C5+ then C5/C6+), verify purity and cost, then optimize severity and consider adding a heavy product only if profitable. Step 9: run moderate 60/70-stage columns at feed pressure.
The C6-paraffin route is unattractive: N-hexane/MCP volatility is close, and extreme severity cost $1.52B/yr without any sale. C5 blend has maximum revenue about $618M/yr and both required splits are much easier. Root now sends C4 and lighter overhead; B isolates isopentane+N-pentane overhead from C6+ bottoms. Moderate reflux/boil-up should sharply reduce duties and refrigeration costs.

note: Move the root split from C5/C6 down to C4/C5 by lowering boil-up, and reduce both columns' size and duties to approach profitability.
notebook:
PLAN: Establish a profitable two-column C5-blend train (C4-/C5+ then C5/C6+), verify purity and cost, then optimize severity and consider heavy products only if profitable. Step 10: move the root cut down to C4 by sharply reducing boil-up and reduce column size/duties.
The C6-paraffin route was unattractive: N-hexane/MCP volatility is close and extreme severity cost $1.52B/yr without sales. C5 blend maximum revenue is about $618M/yr and its two splits are easier. The prior root boil-up of 6 carried most C5 overhead; reducing it to 1.8 should retain C5 in the bottoms. Moderate stages and reflux should cut the very large energy and equipment costs.
